slides.title: No Study Is Perfect
bullets: Systematically identifying a study's limitations and biases is a valuable, rarely-taught MSL skill
Communicating evidence as if it were absolute truth is a mistake
This methodological honesty separates non-promotional scientific communication from a sales pitch

slides.title: Selection and Confounding Bias
bullets: Selection bias happens when recruitment or inclusion criteria produce an unrepresentative sample
This is the classic efficacy-to-effectiveness gap
Confounding bias, especially relevant in observational studies, creates an apparent association that isn't causal
Statistical adjustment and propensity score matching reduce but never fully remove this risk

slides.title: Publication and Measurement Bias
bullets: Publication bias is the well-documented tendency for positive results to get published more often
This skews the available literature toward a rosier picture than reality
Measurement or misclassification bias happens when exposure or outcome is measured inconsistently

slides.title: Subtle Flaws That Still Matter
bullets: Statistical significance and clinical relevance are not the same thing
A differential dropout rate, too-short follow-up, or a per-protocol analysis can soften a conclusion
None of these necessarily invalidate a study, but all deserve mention

slides.title: Read the Limitations Section First
bullets: CONSORT for trials and STROBE for observational studies require an explicit limitations section
A rigorous MSL always reads that section, not just the results summary
That's where the authors themselves acknowledge what their study can and cannot claim

slides.title: Transparency Builds Credibility, It Doesn't Cost It
bullets: Naming a study's limitations strengthens the scientific message rather than weakening it
Experienced HCPs quickly notice when only favorable data gets presented
That omission, even unintentional, damages credibility over time
Transparency is the foundation of long-term trust between Medical Affairs and the medical community

takeaway.title: Naming a study's limitations is what makes Medical Affairs communication trustworthy
bullets: Selection, confounding, publication and measurement bias each distort evidence differently
Statistical significance and clinical relevance are separate questions worth checking every time
Reading and disclosing the limitations section separates scientific communication from a sales pitch
